title: A failed pause-expiry re-apply ends as 'archives exposed, status On, nothing retries'
scenario: Team pauses block_archives for 60 min. At expiry the first PHP hit runs the spec's 'if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply'. The re-apply fails for an ordinary reason: (a) the first hit is WP-CLI or a system-cron `php wp-cron.php` (wp_fix_server_vars() leaves SERVER_SOFTWARE='' so Preflight fails); (b) the lock is held because the platform's hardening:resume-expired call and the visitor-triggered re-apply collide at the same moment (by design they fire together); (c) one loopback times out on a busy shared host; (d) the visitor closes the tab and LiteSpeed aborts the PHP process mid-procedure. Per spec, Rollback 'restores the snapshot' - for a resume the snapshot IS the paused file - and sets rules 'back to the previous desired state' (= true). Crash recovery does the same thing (restores the paused snapshot). pause_until is already null. State is now rules.block_archives=true, no pause, no block in the file. Status derives from desired state ('Desired state stays true; the pause is an overlay') so it reports `on`. hardening:resume-expired fetches status, sees 'not paused', closes the row. Full-site backups stay publicly downloadable indefinitely while the panel shows On - exactly the drjung.ch case, now with a green badge.
evidence: Spec 'Pause' (clear then re-apply), 'Rollback' step 6, 'Crash recovery', Part 2 'if still paused call resume; on success close the row'. Plugin bootstraps on every request type incl. CLI/cron: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/landeseiten-maintenance.php:57-63 and :471.
fix: 1) Never clear pause_until before a verified re-apply; on failure keep it, record resume_failed_at/attempts, retry with backoff, expose status `paused_overdue`. 2) Make rollback direction-aware: for resume (re-adding a block that was already verified on this site at enable time) fail CLOSED - keep the block on rule_ineffective / loopback_blocked / busy and revert only on asset_broken. 3) Store pending.op; crash recovery of a pending resume must roll FORWARD (write the block), not restore the paused snapshot. 4) Status must be computed from the parsed file (managed block present and containing the archive rule) AND the desired state; mismatch = `drift`, never `on`. 5) API closes a pause row only on status=on with file_state=present; anything else stays open and raises a notification after 10 min overdue. 6) Optional hardening: make the pause self-expiring inside the file (mod_rewrite `RewriteCond %{TIME} >YYYYMMDDHHMMSS` + `RewriteRule \.(wpress|...)$ - [F]`, calibrated to server-local time by the probe) so expiry needs no PHP, wp-cron or platform at all.
verifier:
The spec text produces this end state. 'Pause' clears pause_until before the re-apply. On a resume the snapshot is the paused file, so Rollback step 6 restores a file without the archive block, and the 'previous desired state' is still true. Crash recovery restores the same snapshot. Part 2 closes the pause row once status is no longer paused. The spec never says `on` is derived from the file, so rules=true with no pause and no block reports On.

Triggers checked:
- wp_fix_server_vars() defaults SERVER_SOFTWARE to '' (wp-includes/load.php:35-40), so WP-CLI and `php wp-cron.php` loads fail Preflight.
- The plugin boots on every request type (/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/landeseiten-maintenance.php:471).
- A single loopback timeout at the one retry moment is ordinary on shared hosting.
- Sub-case (b), lock collision, is harmless on its own because the winner still applies.

High rather than critical. It needs a failure at the resume moment, and the exposure equals today's unhardened state. The false On badge and the closed backstop row still defeat the feature's purpose.
better_fix:
Keep the reviewer's points 1, 2, 5 and a light version of 4. Drop 3 and 6.

(a) Clear pause_until only after a successful re-apply. While it is expired but not cleared, status is `paused` with pause_overdue, so the API row stays open and the 10-minute command keeps retrying.

(b) Throttle plugin-side retries. Store last_attempt_at before starting, allow one attempt per 5 minutes or more, and skip when PHP_SAPI is 'cli'. Without this, a dead loopback adds N x timeout to every visitor request. The uptime ping to /lsm/v1/health has a 15 s timeout (lsm-api/app/Console/Commands/CheckSiteUptime.php:118-119), so it would also produce false down alerts.

(c) Resume fails closed. The identical block was verified on this host at enable time. Roll back only when the baseline asset goes from 200 to non-200. On probe or loopback errors, keep the block and record a warning.

(d) Status `on` requires the managed block with that rule to be present in the file, which is one small file read. Otherwise report `drift`.

(e) The API closes the row only when status reports on.

With (a), crash recovery needs no pending.op or roll-forward. Restoring the paused snapshot leaves pause_until expired, so the re-apply is retried.

Reject the RewriteCond %{TIME} idea. It puts mod_rewrite into wp-content/.htaccess and brings RewriteEngine/FollowSymLinks 403/500 risks and server-time calibration. Those are new failure modes larger than the one it removes.

title: 'Only URLs below wp-content are affected' is false on disk page caches: .gz rule 403s WP Super Cache/Cache Enabler pages, and the self-test cannot see it
scenario: A) Site uses WP Super Cache (mod_rewrite mode + compression) or Cache Enabler's htaccess snippet. The root rewrite serves /wp-content/cache/supercache/<host>/index-https.html.gz to every gzip-capable anonymous visitor. Enabling block_archives puts `<FilesMatch "\.(wpress|sql|zip|tar|gz|bak)$">` into wp-content/.htaccess; it matches the rewritten target, so homepage and every cached page return 403 for anonymous visitors. Self-test: plugin CSS 200 before/after, .bak probe 403 -> 'Applied and verified'. The team member who clicked is logged in (cookie bypasses the cache) and sees a working site. No rollback ever fires. B) WP Rocket / W3TC disk-enhanced / WP Fastest Cache keep cached HTML in wp-content/cache/...; any wp-content/.htaccess that 500s on that host (e.g. AllowOverride without AuthConfig/Limit - the IfModule guards do not help against that) takes the HOMEPAGE down, not just assets. And if PHP dies between Write and Self-test, anonymous visitors never reach PHP (rewrite -> static file -> 500), so visitor traffic can never trigger crash recovery. Note the spec's cache-buster makes this worse: any query string bypasses rewrite-based page caches, so a cache-busted homepage check goes through PHP and returns 200 while real visitors get 403/500. Same blind spot: legitimate .zip media downloads in uploads start returning 403 to clients' customers.
evidence: Spec 'Never the root file' ('the homepage ... served from the root'), Rules table regex incl. `gz`, Self-test baseline = plugin asset + one uploads image only. Fleet has these caches: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php:25-29 (WP Super Cache), :31-44 (W3TC, WP Fastest Cache), :52-56 (WP Rocket).
fix: Add to baseline and post-write checks: home_url('/') plus one inner page fetched as an anonymous browser - NO query string/cache-buster, `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, no cookies - comparing status and non-empty body before/after. Replace bare `gz` with compound archive forms: `\.(wpress|sql|zip|tar|tgz|bak)$|\.(sql|tar|wpress|bak|zip)\.gz$`. Preflight: detect an active page-cache whose cache dir is under WP_CONTENT_DIR and additionally request one real cached file path. Before enabling block_archives, query attachments for matching extensions and require explicit confirmation listing them. Correct the spec's blast-radius claim.
verifier:
Checked against WP Super Cache source (inc/htaccess.php). Expert mode rewrites to wp-content/cache/supercache/%{SERVER_NAME}/$1/index(-https).html.gz under `RewriteCond %{HTTP:Accept-Encoding} gzip`. Its cache-dir .htaccess has only ForceType/AddEncoding and no allow directive. <FilesMatch> applies to the final filename after the internal redirect. So the `gz` alternative in wp-content/.htaccess returns 403 for cached pages to anonymous gzip clients.

The spec self-test (plugin asset, uploads image, .bak probe) cannot see this. The sentence 'affects only URLs below them; the homepage ... served from the root' is wrong for disk caches served by rewrite: WPSC Expert, W3TC disk-enhanced, WP Fastest Cache, and the Cache Enabler snippet.

Overstated parts:
- WP Rocket serves cache through advanced-cache.php in PHP. As far as I recall, its rewrite-based serving is off by default; I did not re-check that.
- LiteSpeed Cache, as far as I know, keeps its cache outside the docroot.
- W3TC uses a `_gzip` suffix and WPFC has no .gz files. The .gz 403 therefore only hits WPSC Expert with compression or the Cache Enabler snippet, which is rare.
- The 500 variant is caught by the plugin-asset baseline.
- The same manual rule including `gz` is already live on audited sites.

The more likely customer-facing hit is legitimate .zip/.gz media in uploads. wp-content/.htaccess covers uploads, so clients' downloads silently return 403.

Not critical, because the configuration is rare and the change is reversible. It is still an undetected outage for anonymous visitors that reports 'Applied and verified'.
better_fix:
(1) Add home_url('/') to the baseline and the post-write comparison. Fetch it anonymously: no cookies, no query string, default WP Accept-Encoding (which contains gzip). Compare status and non-empty body. This costs one extra loopback and catches both the gz-403 and the 500 variants for any rewrite cache.

(2) Correct the blast-radius sentence in 'Never the root file'.

(3) Status returns a count of attachments with archive mime types or extensions (one COUNT query). The confirm modal shows it as a warning. It does not block and does not list files.

Skip cache-plugin detection, real cached-file path probes and the inner-page fetch.

Leave the regex as it is, or exclude only `\.html\.gz`. The proposed compound list would stop covering plain `db.gz`.

title: Self-test passes without observing anything when loopback is uniformly 403 or the baseline is a CDN HIT
scenario: Site is proxied by Cloudflare with Bot Fight Mode (or host WAF / Wordfence throttling the server's own IP): every loopback request from the server IP with a `WordPress/x.y` UA gets 403. Baseline before = 403 ('recorded, not treated as our failure'), after = 403 -> 'same status' passes; .bak probe = 403 -> 'proves it is effective'. Result 'Applied and verified' although nothing was observed: on an nginx-fronted host the rule is actually ineffective (silently unprotected, status On), and a block that 500s on origin is not detected. Variant: baseline asset is answered from a CDN edge (spec puts the cache-buster only on probes; many CDN configs ignore query strings and request Cache-Control; WP_CONTENT_URL / plugins_url / upload baseurl may point to a CDN or cookieless host, LSM_PLUGIN_URL is derived from plugins_url) -> after-write baseline is a cached 200 while origin returns 500; the breakage surfaces hours later as edge TTLs expire, with no rollback trigger left. Pause on such a site always fails with a misleading pause_ineffective_foreign_rule.
evidence: Spec step 2 ('A non-200 baseline is recorded, not treated as our failure'), step 5 ('Each must return 403', cache-buster only on 'Probe requests'). LSM_PLUGIN_URL = plugin_dir_url(): /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/landeseiten-maintenance.php:25.
fix: Differential test with a positive control: in each target dir create `lsm-ok-<rand>.txt` containing a random token; it must return 200 + the token BEFORE and AFTER the write (random name defeats every cache layer and proves the loopback really reaches this docroot - also catches DNS pointing at another server). The deny probe must return 200 + token BEFORE the write and 403 AFTER; if it is already 403 before, report `foreign_block_or_filtered_loopback` and do not claim verified `on`. Any non-200 positive control = `selftest_inconclusive` -> refuse to write (for enable). Refuse if the probe URL host differs from the home host. Treat responses with cf-cache-status/age/x-cache HIT as inconclusive.
verifier:
This follows directly from the spec. Step 2 accepts a non-200 baseline. Step 5 only requires 'same status' plus a probe 403. A uniformly 403 loopback therefore passes while observing nothing. That happens with Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode or a host WAF against the server IP and the WordPress UA, a known WordPress loopback problem. In that state neither a 500 nor an ineffective rule is detected, and the whole safety promise rests on this test.

A further variant the reviewer missed, verified in the OWASP CRS crs-setup.conf.example: the default tx.restricted_extensions (rule 920440) contains .bak, .sql and .log. It does not contain .zip, .gz, .tar or .wpress. On ModSecurity-CRS hosts the `.bak` probe is 403 before and after, regardless of .htaccess. Enable is then 'verified' vacuously. Every pause fails with pause_ineffective_foreign_rule even though the .wpress download would work, which breaks the core use case.

The CDN-HIT variant is weaker than claimed. The random-named deny probe always reaches origin and returns 500 (not 403) if the block broke the directory. It only matters on paths with no probe: pause/off, and debug_log when no debug.log exists.
better_fix:
No extra lsm-ok files and no CDN-header sniffing.

(1) The baseline plugin asset must be 200 with a non-empty body before any write. Otherwise refuse with loopback_blocked and write nothing. Delete 'a non-200 baseline is recorded'.

(2) Create the deny probe before the write and fetch it, expecting 200 plus the token. After the write expect exactly 403. If it is already 403 before while the baseline is fine, report a foreign/WAF block and do not claim 'verified by us'.

(3) For pause/off require 200 plus the token, not merely 'not 403'.

(4) Use `.wpress` as the archive probe extension. It is the real use case and is not in the CRS list.

(5) Put the cache-buster on all self-test requests, including the baseline.

The random-named probe also serves as the positive control that the loopback reaches this docroot.

title: Every backup made through the pause workflow embeds an expired pause; restoring it triggers an unattended re-apply on the wrong host
scenario: The purpose of Pause is to run an All-in-One WP Migration export. That export dumps the DB while lsm_hardening = {rules.block_archives:true, pause_until:T} (and, if AI1WM packs wp-content/.htaccess, the paused file). Later the .wpress is imported during a host migration (DNS still on the old server), onto a staging subdomain behind basic auth, or the DB alone is restored with mysqldump. First plugin load: pause_until < now -> clear + re-apply inside a front-end/admin request. The loopback self-test resolves home_url to the OLD server (probe files exist only on the new disk -> 404 through WordPress) or gets 401 -> rule_ineffective -> rollback -> end state of finding 1: rules=true, no block, status On - on what becomes the production host after the DNS switch. The platform has no open pause row for it (closed months ago), so no backstop looks.
evidence: Spec State block (pause_until stored in the same DB option as desired rules), 'Pause' ('On every plugin load, if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply'), Problem section (AI1WM download is the use case).
fix: Store an environment fingerprint (home_url + ABSPATH + server hostname hash) alongside the state; on mismatch never auto-write - set status `needs_review` and surface it to the platform. Keep pause_until out of the desired-state option (separate non-autoloaded option) and treat a pause that expired more than ~2 h ago as stale: mark `drift`, do not auto-apply from an arbitrary request. Keep desired rules per project in lsm-api and reconcile from there after restores/migrations.
verifier:
By design, every export made during a pause embeds rules=true plus pause_until, because the pause exists for that export. A restored copy hits 'expired -> clear + re-apply' on its first load.

The unattended apply is harmless in itself. It is the safe procedure, and behind basic auth or pre-switch DNS it simply rolls back. The harmful end state (pause cleared, rules true, no block, no platform row) is the end state of finding 1, reached by another path. It is not an independent defect. It does matter, because a re-apply failure is likely during migrations.
better_fix:
Nothing beyond finding 1. Keep pause_until until a verified re-apply and throttle retries. The site then self-heals after the DNS switch, and status-from-file shows paused-overdue or drift in the meantime.

Environment fingerprint, separate options, a stale-pause rule and API-side desired-state reconciliation are YAGNI for v1.

title: Transient lock is check-then-set, is wiped by the plugin's own cache/transient actions, and snapshot + pending are single slots
scenario: get_transient -> set_transient is not atomic: with Redis/LSCache object cache transients live only in the cache (no add semantics); without one, set_transient -> add_option is INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, so both racers 'acquire'. A collision is built into the design at pause expiry (visitor-triggered re-apply + hardening:resume-expired + user's 'Re-enable now'), plus two team members toggling different rules. Additionally a teammate pressing 'Clear cache' (wp_cache_flush) or 'clear all transients' during the run deletes the lock. Run A writes its block; Run B passes Preflight, overwrites .htaccess.lsm-bak with A's not-yet-tested file and overwrites the single `pending` slot. A's self-test fails -> A 'restores the snapshot' = its own broken file -> a no-op rollback reported as 'Rolled back'; B finishes and clears `pending`, so no recovery flag remains for A. Deactivation and adoption touch two files but `pending` holds one. Separately, the spec maps lock contention to rule status `unsupported`, which the UI renders as 'Not supported'.
evidence: Spec Preflight ('transient lsm_hardening_lock, 120 s ... Any failure -> status unsupported'), Snapshot (fixed name .htaccess.lsm-bak), State (single `pending`). Lock killers: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php:99-103 (wp_cache_flush in clear_cache), /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-api.php:686 and :789-793 (DELETE all _transient_%). The team's own in-progress guard already uses an atomic lock: class-lsm-actions.php:560 (WP_Upgrader::create_lock) in the working tree.
fix: Use `SELECT GET_LOCK('lsm_hardening_<DB_NAME>_<prefix>', 0)` - atomic, auto-released when the PHP process dies (no TTL guessing), immune to cache flush and transient purges; fall back to the WP_Upgrader::create_lock INSERT IGNORE pattern. Per-run snapshot `.htaccess.lsm-bak.<run_id>` and `pending` keyed by file with run_id, existed, orig_sha1, written_sha1; a run only clears its own entry. Lock busy -> HTTP 409 `busy` (retryable), never `unsupported`. In lsm-api wrap all hardening calls per project in Cache::lock.
verifier:
Verified in core:
- set_transient() goes to add_option(), which runs `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` (wp-includes/option.php:664). Both racers succeed.
- With an external object cache, transients live only in the cache (option.php:960).
- clear_cache() calls wp_cache_flush() (/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php:100-101).
- clear_transients with all=true deletes `_transient_%` (class-lsm-api.php:792).

The race window is milliseconds. It is plausible at pause expiry on a busy site, where every request in that instant sees the expired pause. Otherwise it is rare.

The spec wording that maps lock contention to rule status `unsupported` (UI 'Not supported') is a real defect.

Not real: the single-slot snapshot and `pending` are sufficient once the lock is atomic. Each rule lives in exactly one file, adoption rewrites that same file, and deactivation can process its two files sequentially.
better_fix:
Use WP_Upgrader::create_lock('lsm_hardening', ttl) and release_lock. It is an atomic INSERT IGNORE on a non-transient option name, so cache flushes and transient purges cannot remove it. The team already uses this pattern at class-lsm-actions.php:560.

Do not use GET_LOCK. It is connection-scoped and unreliable behind DB proxies on shared hosting.

Lock busy returns success:false with reason `busy` (retryable, API 409). It is never a rule status.

Skip per-run snapshot names, keyed pending and the API-side Cache::lock.

title: Lock TTL, crash-recovery threshold and API timeout are all 120 s with no loopback deadline: recovery races a live run, and the single autoloaded option is written back stale
scenario: Slow shared host: loopbacks take 10-15 s (the codebase's existing loopback uses timeout 15). Baseline 2 + self-test up to 5 + rollback re-baseline 2 = up to 9 calls, about 135 s; socket wait does not count toward max_execution_time, so PHP keeps going. At t=120 s, simultaneously: LsmService::post() gives up and returns null (outcome unknown - for a pause the API will most likely write no project_hardening_pauses row although the plugin completes the pause, so no backstop will ever resume it); the lock expires; the user retries, and the retry's plugin load sees `pending` older than 120 s and restores the snapshot underneath the still-running first request, then starts a second apply. The first request then finishes and update_option()s its in-memory copy of the whole lsm_hardening array (rules, pause_until, pending, last_result are one option read once per request) -> lost update: it reverts the second run's rules, or re-sets a `pending` that was already cleared, and 120 s later crash recovery reverts a verified change while status still says on. The same stale write-back comes from a nested loopback that falls through to WordPress (probe file could not be created -> 404 via index.php -> plugin load inside the locked window).
evidence: Spec Preflight (120 s), Crash recovery (120 s), Part 2 ('POSTs use UPDATE_TIMEOUT (120 s)'), State ('autoloaded, one read per request'). /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:13-14 and post()/handleResponse() ~:655-692 (timeout/exception -> null; on success the `success` key is stripped, so 'check success explicitly' needs care). /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php:676-679 (15 s loopback).
fix: Hard time budget: per-loopback timeout 5 s, abort BEFORE any write when the first baseline is a WP_Error, total deadline 45 s (well below lock, recovery threshold and API timeout). Recovery condition = `pending` set AND lock obtainable (owner is dead), not age. Split state into separate options (rules; pause; pending non-autoloaded; last_result), re-read from DB under the lock before each write, compare run_id before clearing pending. API: treat null/timeout as `unknown` and poll status until pending clears; write the pause row BEFORE calling the plugin (write-ahead) and close/delete it only on a confirmed state.
verifier:
Partly real. The three 120 s values are in the spec and no loopback timeout or total budget is specified. Whether it bites depends on an unstated implementation choice:
- With WP's default 5 s timeout the worst case is about 9 x 5 = 45 s and nothing races.
- With the 15 s already used in the plugin (class-lsm-actions.php:676-678) it reaches about 135 s, and lock expiry, crash recovery and the API timeout coincide.

The stale whole-option write-back only happens when two runs overlap, which means only after the lock expires. It does not come from nested loopbacks. A nested load only reads, `pending` is fresh, and the lock is held.

Real gaps:
- LsmService::post() returns null on timeout or non-2xx (/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:655-679). The spec defines neither the null case nor the ordering of the pause row.
- handleResponse() strips `success` only when a `data` key exists (:684-689). Check `=== false` and do not wrap the response in `data`.
better_fix:
Put numbers in the spec:
- Per-loopback timeout 5 s.
- Abort before any write if the first baseline is a WP_Error.
- Total budget of 60 s or less.
- Lock TTL 180 s.
- Crash-recovery threshold at or above the lock TTL, and recovery must acquire the lock before restoring.

API:
- Insert the pause row before calling the plugin.
- Delete it on an explicit success:false.
- Keep it on null, so the backstop reads status and then closes or resumes.
- Map null to a 502 'outcome unknown, refresh status'.

No option splitting, no run_id, no polling loop.

title: Process killed between Write and Self-test: recovery depends on a later plugin load that cached sites do not produce; PHP probe is left behind
scenario: Enable on a Hostinger/LiteSpeed site. The platform connection drops (LiteSpeed aborts PHP on client disconnect unless noabort is set; mod_fcgid IO timeout; OOM kill) after step 4 and before step 6; `finally` does not run on a kill. On this host the block 500s (AllowOverride restriction). Recovery only happens 'on plugin load' after 120 s: on a WP Rocket site anonymous visitors never reach PHP (finding 2) and the front end is down; on LSCache/CDN-cached sites HTML is 200 but every CSS/JS/image under wp-content is 500. The next guaranteed PHP hit from the platform is the hourly SyncPhpErrorsJob -> up to an hour broken. Separately, uploads/lsm-probe-<rand>.php stays on disk forever: LSM's own scanner reports it as severity high 'PHP file in uploads directory', and Wordfence will too - on a fleet that just had an account-wide breach this triggers incident work.
evidence: Spec steps 4-7 and 'Crash recovery' (only trigger is plugin load); probes deleted 'in a finally'. /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/routes/console.php:132 (hourly job is the most frequent REST hit to every site). /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-security-scanner.php:133-158 (flags any non-whitelisted .php in uploads as high).
fix: Test before touching the live file: write the candidate block to a throwaway canary dir (wp-content/lsm-htcanary-<rand>/.htaccess and the same under uploads) with positive-control and deny probes inside; only if the canary behaves (200/403, no 500) write the real file, then re-verify. A kill mid-procedure then breaks only the canary. Also: ignore_user_abort(true) + set_time_limit at start (as class-lsm-actions.php:575-576 does), register_shutdown_function that rolls back if this run still owns `pending`, record probe/canary paths in `pending` and delete them during recovery, sweep lsm-probe-*/lsm-htcanary-* older than 5 min on every status call. API drives recovery: after any non-definitive response call status at +10/+30/+60 s, and the plugin exposes POST /hardening/recover that restores immediately when pending is set and the lock is free.
verifier:
This needs two independent rare events within a window of a few seconds: the block returns 500 on this host, and PHP is killed between write and test. The client is the platform with a 120 s timeout, so a disconnect in that window is unlikely.

'Up to an hour broken' is wrong. The uptime monitor calls /wp-json/lsm/v1/health, which loads the plugin, every uptime interval. The default is 5 minutes (/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/config/uptime.php:15, app/Console/Commands/CheckSiteUptime.php:118-119). Recovery therefore fires within the threshold plus one interval. The WP Rocket claim is wrong in mechanism (it serves via PHP), but cached hits do skip plugin load.

Correct sub-points:
- `finally` does not run on a kill or fatal timeout.
- A leftover uploads/lsm-probe-*.php is flagged severity high by the plugin's own scanner (class-lsm-security-scanner.php:133-158). That is noisy on a recently breached fleet.
better_fix:
- Call ignore_user_abort(true) and set_time_limit at the start, as class-lsm-actions.php:575-576 does.
- Add a register_shutdown_function that rolls back if this run still owns `pending`.
- Record probe paths in `pending` and delete them in crash recovery. Also sweep lsm-probe-* files older than a few minutes on status calls.

The canary directory is a legitimate optional upgrade. It also removes the seconds of broken assets during an ordinary rollback. It is not required for v1.

The /hardening/recover route and the +10/+30/+60 polling are unnecessary given the uptime ping.

title: Rollback and crash recovery restore a whole-file snapshot, overwriting legitimate edits made since - including days-old stale snapshots
scenario: A) Window inside one run: snapshot of uploads/.htaccess at t0; at t0+3 s an admin enables Wordfence / Sucuri / Really Simple Security 'disable PHP execution in uploads', which rewrites the same file; at t0+20 s our self-test fails -> copy(.lsm-bak -> .htaccess) erases their block while their UI still says protected. B) Stale pending: `pending` is set when the plugin stops loading (fatal + WP recovery-mode pause, plugins folder renamed for troubleshooting, deactivated mid-run). Days later the plugin loads again: 'pending older than 120 s -> restore that file's snapshot' overwrites whatever the SSH audit procedure or a security plugin has since written to wp-content/.htaccess (e.g. the manual archive-deny appended during a cleanup) -> protection silently dropped. 'File did not exist' variant: recovery deletes a file someone else created in the meantime. The spec never deletes .htaccess.lsm-bak at Finish and `pending` has no field for 'did not exist', so recovery can also restore an unrelated older snapshot.

Scenario A needs a third party rewriting the same file inside our 10-20 s run, and our self-test failing. That is negligible.

Scenario B needs a crash mid-run, then the plugin not loading for days, then an edit in between. Also negligible. The consequence is someone's rules silently dropped, and the guard is cheap.

Real spec gaps:
- `pending {file, started_at}` has nowhere to record 'file did not exist', yet steps 3 and 6 depend on it.

- `pending` gains `existed` and `written_sha1`.
- Same-request rollback restores from the in-memory original.
- Crash recovery restores the snapshot only when sha1(current) equals written_sha1. Otherwise it strips only the LSM-HARDENING block and reports that.

Skip run_id, the 1-hour rule and re-inserting adopted manual blocks.

Compute status from the file:

- Block present while desired is off: show on (or drift), so pause stays available.

Resolve paths from WP_CONTENT_DIR and wp_upload_dir()['basedir'].

title: Deactivate/reactivate leaves rules=true with no block; a plugin that stops loading without the hook freezes the file in its current (possibly paused) state

If it was paused, the pause never expires (no plugin load); hardening:resume-expired gets a 404 -> 'unreachable, retry next run' forever with no alert. Status-from-file (as in finding 9) makes this visible as drift. No needs_reapply flag and no auto re-apply are needed.

Add a runbook line for manually removing the `# BEGIN LSM-HARDENING` block.

title: Re-apply and crash recovery run inline at plugin load inside whatever request comes first: visitors, the 30-second status GET, admin-ajax, cron, CLI
scenario: Pause expires; the first PHP request is: (a) a visitor - 6-9 sequential loopback HTTPS calls are added to their page load (seconds normally, n x timeout on a slow host); several simultaneous visitors all enter because the lock is not atomic; (b) the platform's own GET /hardening/status from hardening:resume-expired - the apply runs during plugin load before REST dispatch, the 30 s GET times out -> 'unreachable', row left open, and the following resume() POST runs a second full apply; every other platform call (health-check --deep, SyncPhpErrorsJob) can likewise absorb the apply and time out, producing false health alarms; (c) WP-CLI or CLI cron - SERVER_SOFTWARE empty -> Preflight 'unsupported' (feeds finding 1), and on non-suexec hosts files created as the SSH user are later unwritable for PHP. The work also runs before `init`, i.e. before LSM_Logger::init().
evidence: Spec 'Crash recovery' and 'Pause' ('On every plugin load'). /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/landeseiten-maintenance.php:57-63, :208-227 (LSM_Logger::init at :213), :471. /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:13 (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT 30 for GET).

Execution happens in a dedicated authenticated route (e.g. POST lsm/v1/hardening/tick) called by (1) the platform command as the primary driver - run it every 1-2 min for projects with open pause rows, with an explicit withoutOverlapping(5) expiry given the stuck-mutex history - and (2) a throttled non-blocking self-spawn (wp_remote_post blocking=false) guarded by an atomic spawned_at marker. Never execute in CLI, cron, admin-ajax or front-end context. GET /hardening/status must be side-effect free.
verifier:
The spec literally says 'on every plugin load'. Verified consequences:

(1) If the re-apply runs at include time, step 7's LSM_Logger::log() calls wp_get_current_user() (class-lsm-logger.php:274). That function is pluggable and is only defined after all plugins are included. The result is a fatal on every request. The reviewer's 'before LSM_Logger::init()' point understates this.

(2) A CLI or cron-CLI context fails Preflight, which feeds finding 1.

(3) The uptime monitor hits /lsm/v1/health with a 15 s timeout every interval, and the status GET has 30 s. An inline apply with dead or slow loopbacks exceeds both. That gives false down alerts. If it retries on every load, it adds N x timeout to every visitor request.

On a healthy host the apply takes about 1-3 s, once per pause. The visitor-latency point alone is minor. Several visitors entering at once is finding 5.
better_fix:
No tick route, no self-spawn, no 1-2 minute scheduler. Keep the on-load trigger with these changes:
- Hook on `init`.
- Skip when PHP_SAPI is 'cli'.
- Take the atomic lock first. Losers continue immediately.
- Write last_attempt_at before starting and retry at most every 5 minutes.
- Resume uses the light fail-closed path from finding 1: write plus baseline check, 5 s timeouts, abort on the first WP_Error.

The 10-minute platform command stays as the backstop. It needs an explicit withoutOverlapping(15), not the 24 h default. A stuck default-expiry mutex already blocked the uptime check from 25 to 28 August.

title: insert_with_markers does not behave as the spec assumes: never removes the block, returns true on a short write, rewrites in place, swallows foreign rules when END is missing
scenario: 1) 'An empty rule set removes the block' is false: the function always writes `# BEGIN/END LSM-HARDENING` plus three translated instruction lines (site locale, filterable), so markers stay forever; with 'file did not exist' and all rules off it creates a file; any status or sha1 logic that equates 'marker present' with on, or hashes the block, breaks across locales. 2) It returns (bool)$bytes: under quota/disk-full (this fleet has filled quotas with orphaned backup zips before) a short fwrite returns >0, ftruncate cuts at the short length, and the function returns TRUE with a file cut mid-directive (unclosed <FilesMatch>) -> 500 under wp-content. The snapshot copy() under the same quota yields a 0-byte/partial .lsm-bak which rollback then copies over the real file, erasing pre-existing rules. Preflight is_writable() does not see quota. 3) fseek(0)+fwrite+ftruncate is an in-place rewrite: concurrent asset requests can read a half-written file. 4) If the END marker is missing (truncation, hand edit), every line after BEGIN is treated as ours and dropped - and the audit procedure APPENDS manual rules, i.e. after our block.
evidence: WordPress core wp-admin/includes/misc.php insert_with_markers() (verified in a local 6.1.1 copy: instruction lines merged at :137-169, marker split loop :196-212, write/return :235-246). Spec step 3 (no snapshot verification), step 4 ('An empty rule set removes the block').

Really remove block and markers when the rule set is empty, and delete the file if it is then empty and did not exist before. Verify snapshot sha1 == original sha1 before writing, else abort with `snapshot_failed`. Parse markers strictly: BEGIN without END -> abort with `markers_corrupt`, write nothing.
verifier:
Verified in core 6.1.1 (/Users/bmarkovic/Local Sites/loanable/app/public/wp-admin/includes/misc.php:113-247):
- It always writes BEGIN/END plus three localized, filterable instruction lines (:137-169). 'An empty rule set removes the block' is false, and it creates a file where none existed.
- It returns (bool)$bytes after ftruncate at ftell (:235-246). A short write returns true.
- BEGIN without END puts every following line into $existing_lines (:196-212), and those lines are replaced.

Calibration:
- Leftover comment-only markers are harmless to Apache. They still break the planned 'marker removal' tests, deactivation's 'removes both managed blocks', and any marker-presence or sha1 logic.
- A short write needs quota exhaustion exactly at a block boundary. The resulting 500 is caught by the self-test. The real danger is a failed or partial snapshot under the same quota being copied back, and this fleet has had full quotas.
- A missing END needs prior corruption.
- The in-place rewrite race is theoretical. Core does the same on the root .htaccess.
better_fix:
A small own writer is justified, because true removal is needed anyway:
- Read the file into memory.
- Parse markers strictly. BEGIN without END, or duplicates, aborts with `markers_corrupt` and writes nothing.
- Build the content and write with file_put_contents(LOCK_EX).
- Re-read and compare sha1. On mismatch, restore from memory.

Snapshot: require copy()===true and sha1 equal to the original before writing, otherwise `snapshot_failed`.

On an empty rule set remove the markers too. Delete the file if it is then empty and did not exist before.

temp+rename is optional. It changes inode, owner and perms, and is unnecessary for a file under 4 KB.

title: A failed or raced auto-resume rolls back to the exposed (paused) file, clears the pause flag, and nothing retries or alerts
scenario: Rollback is direction-blind: for a resume, the snapshot taken in step 3 IS the paused, unprotected file. Sequence: developer pauses 60 min. At expiry the first plugin load clears pause_until (spec: 'clear it and re-apply') and runs the full apply inside a front-end visitor request. On shared hosting the loopback self-test fails at that moment (Hostinger 508 entry-process limit under bot load, WAF rate-limiting the server's own IP, transient 5xx). Step 6 restores the snapshot = file without the archive block, rules stays true, pause_until is already null. Status is no longer 'paused', so hardening:resume-expired ('if still paused call resume') does not call resume and closes or ignores the row. Backups stay public indefinitely with the card showing On (if derived from the option) or Off with nobody notified. Extra triggers built into the design: (a) at expiry every concurrent visitor plus the platform cron see pause_until passed at once; the transient lock is not atomic (get/set TOCTOU, worse with a persistent object cache) and the snapshot has one fixed name, so apply B can snapshot/roll back over apply A that already reported success to the platform; (b) lock TTL, crash-recovery threshold and platform UPDATE_TIMEOUT are all 120 s, so an apply with slow loopbacks (up to ~7 requests) that runs past 120 s gets 'crash-recovered' by another visitor's request mid-flight - snapshot restored while the first apply then finishes and reports success.
fix: Make apply direction-aware. A tightening write (enable, resume, expiry re-apply) is rolled back only on asset_broken or write failure; on loopback_blocked / probe inconclusive keep the protective block in the file and report 'on_unverified'. Do not clear pause_until until a local read-back confirms the block is in the file (no HTTP needed). Add an explicit plugin status such as resume_failed/exposed that the platform cron treats exactly like paused (retry + alert). Use an atomic lock (WP_Upgrader::create_lock style INSERT, which the in-progress update guard already uses) instead of a transient. Do not run the HTTP self-test on front-end visitor requests: on expiry from a visitor request do the cheap local write + read-back only, leave verification to the platform cron. Set crash-recovery threshold well above lock/timeout (e.g. 300 s) and have the running apply refresh pending.started_at.
evidence: Spec 'Pause': 'On every plugin load, if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply'; 'Apply procedure' step 6 'Any failed check -> restore the snapshot'; 'If loopback requests ... are blocked ... the change is rolled back'; Part 2 'if still paused call resume'. Lock = transient lsm_hardening_lock 120 s; crash recovery 'older than 120 s'; /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:14 UPDATE_TIMEOUT = 120. Atomic lock precedent: uncommitted diff in /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php (WP_Upgrader::create_lock('lsm_bulk_plugin_update')).
verifier:
Confirmed against the spec text. Step 6 restores the snapshot on ANY failed check, and for resume or expiry the snapshot from step 3 is the paused file, which has no archive block. 'Pause' says 'if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply'. Step 6 resets only `rules`, which stays true, and never restores pause_until. After one transient loopback failure at resume time (5xx, 508, timeout) the state is rules=true, pause_until=null, and no archive block in the file. Part 2's cron only acts 'if still paused', so nothing retries and nothing alerts. If status comes from the option, the card shows On. Crash recovery restores the same exposed snapshot if the crash happens during a resume.

The sub-claims are valid but secondary:
- The transient lock is a get/set TOCTOU. An atomic precedent exists in the uncommitted diff of `/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-actions.php` (`WP_Upgrader::create_lock`).
- Lock TTL, crash threshold and `UPDATE_TIMEOUT` (`/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:14`) are all 120 s, so a slow apply can be 'crash-recovered' mid-flight. This only bites if per-request timeouts are set high; WP's default is 5 s.

Downgraded from critical. It needs a coincident self-test failure, and the end state equals today's unhardened baseline. But it is silent and indefinite, and it is the one path where the feature is worse than the manual rule. It must be fixed in the spec before implementation.
better_fix:
The proposed fix is the right direction but adds two new statuses and more machinery than needed. A simpler version, which is actually less code than the spec:
1. A resume or expiry re-apply rewrites a block that already passed the self-test at enable time. Its success criterion is write plus local read-back (`extract_from_markers`), with no HTTP and no probe-based rollback. This also removes loopbacks and self-tests from unauthenticated visitor requests.
2. Clear pause_until only AFTER read-back confirms the block. On write failure keep the expired pause_until, so status stays `paused` with `pause_overdue` and the existing cron keeps retrying. No new status is needed.
3. `pending` records op=resume. Crash recovery for a resume re-applies the block instead of restoring the snapshot.
4. Use an atomic lock: `WP_Upgrader::create_lock`, or a 5-line `add_option` lock on front-end loads.
5. Cap each loopback at about 8 s so the whole apply stays under 60 s, and set the crash threshold to 600 s. No `started_at` refresh is needed.

title: Self-test can report 'Applied and verified' for a rule that does nothing: no control probe, and debug.log is never probed when absent
scenario: The spec tolerates a non-200 baseline ('recorded, not treated as our failure') and only requires that probes return 403. On a site behind Cloudflare Bot Fight Mode / a host WAF that answers 403 to requests from the server's own IP or the WordPress UA, baseline = 403, post-write baseline = 403 (same, passes), every probe = 403 (passes). Result toast: 'Applied and verified'. If that host ignores .htaccess (the audit notes record exactly this for Hostinger H5G: 'ignores .htaccess ENTIRELY ... 2.2 GB of .wpress archives stayed downloadable with a textbook Require all denied'), the team now believes backups are protected while they are public to everyone whose request is not bot-blocked. Second hole: block_debug_log is probed 'only if one exists'. Enable it alone on such a host with no debug.log present -> no probe at all -> status On; later someone flips the platform's debug_enabled toggle, debug.log appears and is world-readable (paths, SQL, sometimes PII) under a green tag.
fix: Differential test: alongside each probe create a control file with a non-blocked extension (lsm-probe-<rand>.txt) in the same directory; the rule is 'verified' only if control = 200 with the expected random body AND probe = 403. Control not 200 -> loopback_blocked/unverifiable (not success). Also run the probe once BEFORE the write; if it is already 403 mark the rule 'on (blocked upstream, unverified)' instead of verified. For debug.log, write the rule as FilesMatch "debug\.log$" and always probe with lsm-probe-<rand>.debug.log so it is verifiable without a real debug.log. On 'must NOT return 403' (pause) require 200 + body token, not merely non-403.

Platform debug toggle: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/LsmController.php:931-939 ('debug_enabled').
verifier:
Real per the spec text. Step 2 says 'A non-200 baseline is recorded, not treated as our failure'. Step 5 requires 'same status as before' and 'probes = 403'. A loopback that gets a uniform 403 (host WAF, Cloudflare bot rules, or a security plugin blocking the server IP or the WordPress UA) passes every check vacuously, and the toast says 'Applied and verified'. Whether the rule really works is then unknown. It does not work on hosts that ignore .htaccess, such as the Hostinger H5G case in `/Users/bmarkovic/.claude/skills/wordpress-security-audit/scripts/wp_audit_scan.sh:794-800`. Medium rather than high: it needs the conjunction of uniform-403 loopback and an ineffective rule, and on a host that simply ignores .htaccess the probes return 200, which the spec already catches.

The debug.log hole is real but small. With block_debug_log enabled alone and no file present there is zero HTTP verification.

The reviewer's trigger for that hole is WRONG. The platform's `debug_enabled` toggle only stores the option `lsm_debug_preference` (`/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-api.php:1953-1958`). Keep the core of the proposed fix and drop the rest.
1. A positive control must be 200 or the result is `loopback_blocked`. Either require the plugin-asset baseline to be 200, or create an `lsm-probe-<rand>.txt` control beside each probe. The control file is uniform and removes the 'find an existing uploads image' lookup.
2. For debug.log, always request `/wp-content/debug.log` whether it exists or not and expect 403. Apache evaluates authz before the 404, the same mechanism the team's `probe.php` check relies on. Switch to the suffix-pattern plus probe-file variant only if the LiteSpeed verification site answers 404.
3. On pause, require 200 on the probe, not merely 'not 403'.

Drop the pre-write probe and the 'on (blocked upstream, unverified)' status. The spec already accepts foreign rules as `on` and handles them at pause time.

title: Pause exposes every archive type across all of wp-content, is renewable forever by any developer, and the window is observable from outside
scenario: The pause regenerates the block 'with block_archives omitted', so for up to 60 min not only the one .wpress but every .sql/.zip/.tar/.gz/.bak under wp-content is public: guessable names bots brute-force all day (wp-content/backup.zip, uploads/dump.sql, db_*.sql / clean_*.tar.gz left by our own cleanups if they sit under wp-content). For .wpress the audit notes already say the random token 'leaks via logs/referrers'; older AI1WM builds that agencies pin used a 3-digit suffix after a timestamp (to verify against fleet versions), and the natural workflow is create backup -> pause -> download, so the timestamp is within minutes of the pause. The window is externally detectable: with the rule on, Apache answers 403 for any *.wpress name even if the file does not exist (the team's own procedure relies on this with probe.php); during a pause the same URL turns 404. A watcher polling /wp-content/x.wpress knows the minute a pause opens. Nothing limits repetition: pauseHardening = anyone with 'update' (developers), allowed again the moment the previous pause ends (or while paused - spec undefined), so a developer or a stolen developer session keeps the rule effectively off permanently without the admin-only disable ability, and a holder of X-LSM-Key can do the same directly against the plugin with no platform row at all.
fix: During a pause do not drop the rule; regenerate it without 'wpress' only (keep sql|zip|tar|gz|bak denied) and probe with a .wpress probe. Enforce in the PLUGIN (not just the platform): minutes in {15,30,60}, pause-while-paused rejected or capped to 60 min from the first pause, and a cumulative cap per 24 h (e.g. 120 min) after which only an admin-flagged call succeeds. Platform: notify admins on every pause and on overdue, show cumulative pause time on the card. Optional stronger variant: instead of opening to the world, write 'Require ip <acting user IP>' for wpress (IP passed by the platform, validated with FILTER_VALIDATE_IP and nothing else ever interpolated), falling back to the narrowed public pause only when the download still 403s (proxy/CDN in front).

Observed name format: audits/drjung.ch_2026-09-10/findings.json:255 (www-drjung-ch-20260818-184733-gy1wghoqtmkm.wpress). Developer reach: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Policies/ProjectPolicy.php update().

Partly real.

True per spec: pause omits the whole block_archives rule, so .sql, .zip, .tar, .gz and .bak also open for up to 60 min, although the only stated use case is the AI1WM `.wpress` download. Pause-while-paused is undefined.

Not a meaningful threat: 'renewable forever by a developer or stolen session'. Anyone with `update` can already mint a WP administrator SSO link. `/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/LsmController.php:115-129` uses `Gate::authorize('update')` with role defaulting to 'administrator'. The X-LSM-Key holder can do the same directly against the plugin. Both dominate pausing a deny rule. The matrix is a guardrail, not a boundary.

Minutes in {15,30,60} is already specified plugin-side ('allowed values 15, 30, 60'). The 403-to-404 observability leaks nothing without the 12-character random filename. The '3-digit suffix in old AI1WM' claim is unverified for this fleet. The cumulative 24 h cap and the `Require ip` variant are overkill. Take only the near-free parts:

title: Crash recovery restores whatever sits at a DB-supplied path from a never-deleted, fixed-name snapshot: planted or stale .htaccess.lsm-bak becomes live config written by our plugin
scenario: (1) pending = {file, started_at} lives in an autoloaded option. Anyone with option-write (SQLi / arbitrary-option-update bug in any third-party plugin on 100+ sites, or a DB/AI1WM restore carrying an old lsm_hardening row) sets pending.file to an arbitrary path with started_at in the past; the next plugin load 'restores that file's snapshot' or, with the 'file did not exist' flag, DELETES it - wp-config.php deletion is the classic route to reinstall takeover. (2) The spec never deletes the snapshot (step 7 only clears pending) and never says a failed snapshot copy aborts the write. The sc_ kit on this fleet writes 'php_value auto_prepend_file' into wp-content/.htaccess. Enable hardening on a not-yet-detected infected site -> the directive is preserved in .htaccess.lsm-bak; cleanup later fixes .htaccess, but audit A2.3/A2.4 only read files named .htaccess, and A1.11 only looks at wp-content depth 1, so uploads/.htaccess.lsm-bak is invisible to the audit. An attacker who wants persistence plants a read-only (0444, a permission trick already seen on dirr-reisen.de) .htaccess.lsm-bak containing AddHandler/auto_prepend_file; copy() onto it fails, an implementation in the house style (unchecked file_put_contents) proceeds, any later self-test failure 'restores the snapshot' = our trusted plugin installs attacker config right after a cleanup. Stale pending can also resurface without an attacker through the alloptions object-cache race on autoloaded options. (3) On every hardened site the wp-content snapshot trips our own audit A1.11 as a HIGH kit-marker dotfile; whitelisting the name would hand malware a hiding place. Readability over HTTP relies on the server's stock '^\.ht' deny - unverified for Hostinger LiteSpeed and for hosts that ignore .htaccess, where after a rule_ineffective rollback the file is left behind; our own rule does not cover it ('.lsm-bak' does not match '\.bak$').

Same-request rollback uses the original bytes held in memory; the on-disk snapshot exists only while pending is set, is deleted in Finish and after rollback, and pending stores its sha256 - crash recovery restores only on hash match, otherwise it strips the LSM-HARDENING marker block and records snapshot_tampered. Abort before the write if the snapshot cannot be written and read back identically; refuse symlinks (is_link) for both target and snapshot. 'File did not exist' rollback deletes only if the file consists solely of our marker block. Self-test also requests the snapshot URL and requires non-200. Add .htaccess.lsm-bak to the audit's A2.4 grep rather than to A1.11's allow-list.

- An attacker with arbitrary option write already owns the site (`users_can_register` plus `default_role=administrator`).
- An attacker who can plant a 0444 `.htaccess.lsm-bak` can write `.htaccess` directly.
Those parts are not real escalations.

The hygiene residue is real and verified.
1. The spec never deletes the snapshot; step 7 only clears `pending`. So `wp-content/.htaccess.lsm-bak` persists on every hardened site. `/Users/bmarkovic/.claude/skills/wordpress-security-audit/scripts/wp_audit_scan.sh:288` excludes only the exact names `.htaccess` and `.litespeed_conf.dat`, so the team's own audit flags it as a HIGH A1.11 kit-marker dotfile on every hardened site. HTTP readability of the snapshot is low risk. Stock Apache denies `.ht*`, and it becomes moot once the file is short-lived.

2. `pending` stores an enum (content|uploads) plus the op, never a path. Derive paths from `WP_CONTENT_DIR` and `wp_upload_dir()`.

Skip sha256 and tamper detection, symlink checks, the 'delete only if solely our block' rule, a snapshot-URL probe, and audit-script changes. The audit change is unnecessary once the file is transient.

title: Desired state is reported as truth: nothing detects that the managed block is gone (malware rewrite, AI1WM restore, deactivate/reactivate)

title: Rule patterns are case-sensitive and end-anchored, and later/nested config overrides them, yet the lowercase root-level probe still says 'verified'
scenario: block_uploads_php as specified denies .php/.phtml/.php5/.php7/.phar. FilesMatch is case-sensitive while mod_mime handler mapping (AddHandler/AddType, the usual shared-host setup) is case-insensitive and multi-extension: shell.PHP, x.pHp, x.pht, x.php8, x.phps, or x.php.jpg under AddHandler execute. Same for archives: backup.ZIP, dump.SQL, site.tgz, db.sql.bz2, .7z, .rar are served. Overrides: Files sections merge in order, so an attacker whitelist appended after our marker block (audit A2.3 'attacker PHP whitelist') or a nested uploads/2026/09/.htaccess with 'Require all granted', SetHandler or 'AddHandler cgi-script' + ExecCGI (audit A6.5: 'denying PHP in uploads does nothing here') wins. The probe is a lowercase random name in the directory root, so it returns 403 and the card reads On/verified while the attacker's shell runs.

On enable and on every status read, scan the two target files outside our markers, plus nested .htaccess files under uploads (bounded depth/count), for Require all granted / Allow from / Satisfy any / SetHandler / AddHandler / AddType / Options +ExecCGI / auto_prepend_file and surface 'overridden_by_foreign_rule' with the path instead of plain On. FilesMatch regexes are case-sensitive. mod_mime handler mapping is not: 'The extension argument is case-insensitive' (https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/mod_mime.html). The same page documents that with multiple extensions the handler wins, which is the x.php.jpg case. On AddHandler/AddType hosts (cPanel-style shared hosting) shell.PHP, x.pHp and x.php.jpg execute and are not matched by the spec's `\.php$`-style pattern. Host mappings commonly include extensions missing from the spec list, such as .php8 and .pht. The attacker controls the filename in an arbitrary-upload bug, so this is a direct bypass of the control while the lowercase probe still reports 'verified'. The same case issue applies to backup.ZIP and dump.SQL.

The override part is not worth acting on. An attacker who can write a nested .htaccess or append to ours already has file-write. It cannot be fixed from .htaccess (AllowOverride), and finding it is the audit's job (A2.3, A6.5).
better_fix:
Pattern change only, at zero cost.
- Uploads: `(?i)\.(php[0-9]?|phtml?|pht|phps|phar)(\.|$)`
- Archives: `(?i)\.(wpress|sql|zip|tar|gz|bak)$`. Optionally add tgz, bz2, 7z and rar; that list is an owner decision.

PCRE inline `(?i)` is accepted by Apache, and `(?i:` has been seen in the wild on a fleet LiteSpeed host (`wp_audit_scan.sh:757-760`). If a server chokes on it, the existing self-test rolls back. Keep manual-block recognition matching the old exact text.

Skip scanning nested or foreign .htaccess on status reads, and skip the uppercase probe variant.

title: Admin-only 'disable' is not a boundary: one endpoint carries two abilities on a loosely typed flag, and the key/SSO paths skip the matrix entirely
scenario: POST .../hardening/rule {rule, enabled} must pick enableHardening vs disableHardening from 'enabled'. House style forwards raw input with no validation (updateSecuritySettings passes $request->only(...) straight through) and the plugin has zero REST arg schemas and casts with (bool). A manager sends {"enabled":"false"}: a truthiness check on the platform selects the enable gate (non-empty string), the raw string is forwarded, and a plugin that sanitises with rest_sanitize_boolean / a 'type: boolean' schema reads false -> rule removed by a manager. With the opposite pairing the reverse mismatch appears; either way authorisation and effect are decided by two different parsers. Independently: any 'update' holder can mint a WP administrator SSO link and deactivate the plugin in wp-admin (deactivation strips both blocks, no self-test, no platform record); and anyone holding X-LSM-Key (still accepted as ?key= in URLs, i.e. in access logs of shared accounts) calls the plugin's /hardening/rule directly.

With idiomatic Laravel (`$request->boolean()` and the `boolean` validation rule) "false" is handled or rejected correctly. The bypass needs one sloppy side and one strict side. Still, the spec hangs an authz decision on a request field and says nothing about validation. The cited precedent is real: `/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/LsmController.php:921-947` does a raw `$request->only()` passthrough, the plugin uses `(bool)` casts at `class-lsm-api.php:1933-1964`, and there are no `args` schemas anywhere in the file.
