title: Cross-lens: block_archives denies legitimate .gz/.zip served from wp-content and the self-test cannot see it
scenario: The rule matches by extension anywhere under wp-content. WP Super Cache in mod_rewrite mode internally rewrites page requests to wp-content/cache/supercache/<host>/.../index-https.html.gz; the internal redirect is subject to wp-content/.htaccess, so gzip-accepting visitors (all browsers) get 403 on cached pages while the self-test (one plugin asset + probe) passes and the toast says 'Applied and verified'. Same for client download areas with .zip files in uploads and WooCommerce 'redirect only' downloads. To be confirmed on a test site, but the check is cheap.
fix: Before enabling, scan for served archive types: root .htaccess rewrite targets ending in .gz, and count of .zip/.gz under uploads (excluding backup dirs); show them in the confirm modal and require explicit acknowledgement. Add the homepage (cache-busted AND a plain cached request with Accept-Encoding: gzip) to the baseline/self-test set for the wp-content file.
evidence: Spec 'Rules' table and step 2 baseline (plugin asset + one uploads image only).
verifier:
The mechanism is sound under Apache semantics. WP Super Cache in Expert (mod_rewrite) mode internally redirects page requests to `wp-content/cache/supercache/<host>/.../index-https.html.gz`. The internal redirect re-runs the directory and file walk, so the FilesMatch `\.gz$` deny inherited from wp-content/.htaccess applies. Gzip-capable visitors get 403 on cached pages. Cache Enabler's optional Apache snippet behaves the same way. WP Rocket and W3TC use `.html_gzip` and are not matched.

The self-test (one plugin asset plus probes) cannot see this. It contradicts the spec's promise that a bad rule cannot take a site down, and its 'homepage is served from the root' assumption.

Media-library .zip downloads (press kits, forms bundles) on client sites would also silently return 403.

Scope is limited to specific cache modes and sites, and whether the fleet has any is unknown. The manual rule has the same pattern and has apparently not bitten yet. Medium is right.

Parsing root .htaccess rewrite targets and crawling uploads is heavier than needed.
better_fix:
1. Add the homepage to the wp-content baseline as a PLAIN request: no query string and no cookies. Supercache rules require an empty QUERY_STRING, and the WP HTTP API already sends Accept-Encoding gzip. A 200-to-403 or 5xx change after the write is `asset_broken` and rolls back. This also makes the 'site still renders' check real. The nested loopback request loads the plugin, which is safe provided lock acquisition is non-blocking.
2. The status response includes a count of media-library attachments with zip or gzip mime types. That is one `wp_posts` query. The confirm modal warns 'N downloadable archives in the media library will stop working'.

No .htaccess rewrite parsing and no filesystem crawl.

title: A failed re-apply at pause expiry leaves the site unprotected while plugin status, pauses table and watchdog all report 'fine'
scenario: Dev pauses block_archives for 60 min on a WP-Rocket-cached Hostinger site. At expiry the first PHP hit runs the spec's 'clear pause_until and re-apply'. The apply fails for a transient reason (loopback times out because PHP workers are saturated, lock held by a second concurrent plugin load, file perms). Step 6 rollback restores the snapshot = the PAUSED file (no archive block) and 'sets rules back to the previous desired state' = block_archives:true (pause is only an overlay). Result: pause_until=null, rules.block_archives=true, file has no block. Nothing ever retries because pause_until is already cleared. hardening:resume-expired fetches status, sees 'not paused', closes the row. Panel shows On. .wpress backups stay publicly downloadable indefinitely. Additionally the spec maps lock contention to status 'unsupported', so two simultaneous plugin loads at expiry (uptime check + panel GET) make the loser record 'unsupported' for a rule that is merely busy.
evidence: Spec 'Pause': 'On every plugin load, if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply'; 'Rollback': 'restore the snapshot ... set rules back to the previous desired state'; Part 2: 'fetch status; if still paused call resume; on success close the row'; Preflight: 'lock acquired ... Any failure -> ... rule status unsupported'. Fleet: WP Rocket active on 125/141 sites (/Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/wp-audits/plugin-inventory-2026-09-14/plugins.csv).
fix: Treat resume as a state machine: pause_until is cleared ONLY after a verified successful re-apply. On failure keep state 'resume_failed' (still reported as paused + overdue), retry with backoff on subsequent loads and on every platform resume call, never roll a resume back to the unprotected file unless the baseline asset check itself broke. Status must expose `effective`/`block_present` derived from the file, and the platform command must close a row only when status says rule desired=on AND block present AND not paused. Lock-busy must be a retryable `busy` result that never changes rule status.
verifier: Traced against the spec text; nothing in the spec prevents it. 'Pause' says 'if pause_until has passed, clear it and re-apply', which clears first. Step 6 rolls back to the snapshot, and on a resume the snapshot is the paused file without the archive block. It also resets `rules` to the previous desired state, which stays block_archives:true because the pause is only an overlay. After one failed resume the state is pause_until=null, rules=on, and a file with no archive block. Nothing retries, and the watchdog sees 'not paused' and closes the row. Transient failures at that moment are normal. Loopback timeouts happen on shared hosts. LiteSpeed also kills the PHP process when the client disconnects (official LSWS docs, see 'missed'), which lands in crash recovery and restores the same paused snapshot. The lock-busy point is also literally in the spec: Preflight lists 'lock acquired' and 'Any failure -> rule status unsupported'. With 'every plugin load' as the trigger, concurrent attempts at expiry are the normal case. The WP Rocket 125/141 figure is verified in plugins.csv. I rate this high, not critical. It needs a failure at resume time, and last_result.ok=false would still be visible. It is still the one path where the feature leaves a site less protected than the manual rule did while the panel reports On.
better_fix:
No new state machine is needed. A pause_until in the past already is the 'resume failed' state.
1. Clear pause_until only after a successful re-apply. Treat expiry as level-triggered: while pause_until < now, retry, throttled by a last_attempt_at field to about once per 5 min. Report the rule as paused plus overdue with last_result.reason.
2. On resume or expiry, roll back only for asset_broken. If the probe or loopback fails, leave the managed block in place, since it was verified when it was enabled, and record a warning. Never restore the unprotected file because a probe timed out.
3. A busy lock is a no-op result ('busy'). It never sets 'unsupported' and never overwrites last_result.
4. The watchdog closes a row only from a resume POST response that says not paused and block present (see host-cached-status-get).

title: Expiry re-apply and crash recovery run inline inside whatever request loads the plugin — in practice the platform's 15 s uptime /health probe
scenario: On cached sites the request that actually executes PHP every 5 min is the platform's own uptime probe to /wp-json/lsm/v1/health (15 s timeout, pooled). With the spec's 'on every plugin load' hook (plugin bootstraps on init priority 0), that probe now performs lock + 2 baseline loopbacks + insert_with_markers + up to 3 probe loopbacks (+ rollback + re-baseline) before answering. On a slow shared host each loopback needs a second PHP worker while the first is held; total easily exceeds 15 s -> uptime records a timeout; if the re-apply keeps failing and is retried on each load, the second consecutive failure fires SiteDownNotification for a healthy site. The same inline work can land on a visitor's uncached POST (contact form, checkout). If the uptime client disconnects and PHP is aborted mid-write, 'pending' stays set and the 120 s crash-recovery path is triggered by the next uptime probe, again inline.
evidence: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Console/Commands/CheckSiteUptime.php:50 (timeout 15), :118-120 (health URL), :396/:462 (second consecutive failure -> notify); config/uptime.php:15,23; /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/landeseiten-maintenance.php:103 (init @0). The in-flight update guard already had to add ignore_user_abort(true)+set_time_limit(0) for the same reason (git diff master -- includes/class-lsm-actions.php on fix/concurrent-plugin-update-guard).
fix: Plugin load must only DETECT (cheap autoloaded option compare) and then hand off: fire a non-blocking authenticated loopback (`wp_remote_post(..., ['blocking'=>false])`) to a dedicated `/hardening/tick` endpoint, or run on `shutdown` after fastcgi_finish_request/litespeed_finish_request. Never apply inside /health, REST status GETs or front-end requests. Make the platform command the primary resumer and the load hook the fallback. Set ignore_user_abort(true) inside apply, and bound the whole apply to a fixed budget (e.g. 5 s per loopback, 45 s total).
verifier:
The mechanism is real. The plugin boots on init@0 (landeseiten-maintenance.php:103), and the spec puts the full apply on 'every plugin load'. That is 2 baseline requests, the write, up to 3 probes and a re-baseline, so 5-9 loopbacks. On a fully cached WP Rocket site the platform's own /health probe is a likely trigger (CheckSiteUptime.php:118-120, 15 s timeout).
The severity is overstated. The re-apply runs once per pause expiry, not on every probe. A healthy apply takes 1-3 s. The uptime state machine needs two consecutive failures before it notifies (CheckSiteUptime.php:370-415), so one slow probe is at worst a 'confirming' blip. Crash recovery is a file copy, not loopbacks, so the '120 s path again inline' part costs nothing.
The abort risk is real on LiteSpeed. LSWS kills the PHP process when the client disconnects and does not honour ignore_user_abort (https://docs.litespeedtech.com/lsws/cp/cpanel/long-run-script/). That makes the proposed fix wrong for a large part of the fleet. A non-blocking loopback (blocking=false) disconnects immediately, which is the wp-cron pattern LSWS documents as getting killed unless the host sets noabort. ignore_user_abort(true) does nothing on LSWS.
better_fix:
Keep the detection on plugin load, a cheap compare on the autoloaded option. Run the actual re-apply on `shutdown` at late priority, after fastcgi_finish_request() or litespeed_finish_request() where those exist. wp-cron.php already does this. The visitor or uptime probe gets its response first. The connection ends normally, so LSWS has nothing to abort.
Bound every loopback (timeout 5 s, sslverify false) so a worst-case apply takes about 45 s, well under the platform's 120 s.
Do not add a /hardening/tick endpoint, a non-blocking loopback, or a rule that the platform command is the primary resumer. The watchdog stays a backstop. Its resume POST is a normal blocking call with a 120 s client, and that is the safe context.

title: Status GET will be served from host cache on some sites (max-age=2419200): stale panel forever and the watchdog closes rows on a lie
scenario: meister-baukonzepte.de (project 173): hosting caches plugin REST GETs for 28 days; this already made backup/list show deleted files until a manual ?nocache= was added. With the spec: (1) user enables a rule, POST returns On, page reload GET returns the cached pre-enable 'off' -> user clicks enable again / believes site is unprotected; (2) user pauses; hardening:resume-expired does 'fetch status; if still paused call resume' -> cached status from before the pause says 'on', command closes the row without resuming; if the plugin-side expiry also fails (finding 1) nobody knows. The panel's pause countdown and pause_overdue are equally frozen.
evidence: LsmService::get() sends no cache-buster: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/app/Services/LsmService.php:638-653. Plugin key-auth is not a logged-in WP user so core sends no no-cache headers; the only nocache_headers() call is class-lsm-support.php:440; authenticate() at class-lsm-api.php:373-401. Incident note: memory project_auto_backups_disabled.md ('meister-baukonzepte.de (173) hosting kesira REST GET cache-control: max-age=2419200 ... sa ?nocache= prazno').
fix: Plugin: every hardening response calls nocache_headers() and adds `Cache-Control: no-store, private` plus a `generated_at` timestamp. API: getHardeningStatus() appends a unique query param and rejects a payload whose generated_at is older than ~60 s (report `status_stale`). The resume command must not decide from a GET at all: always POST /hardening/resume (idempotent no-op when not paused, returns fresh status) and close the row from that POST's response.
verifier:
This is confirmed by the team's own incident. The memory note project_auto_backups_disabled.md records meister-baukonzepte.de (173) caching REST GETs with `cache-control: max-age=2419200`, so backup/list kept showing deleted files until ?nocache= was added. The code matches. LsmService::get() (LsmService.php:638-653) sends no cache-buster. Key-auth never logs in a WP user, so core's rest_send_nocache_headers stays false. The only nocache_headers() call in the plugin is class-lsm-support.php:440.
Both consequences follow from the spec: a stale panel after a POST, and 'fetch status; if still paused call resume' deciding from a cached 'on'. There is one known site and possibly a few unknown ones. The plugin-side self-resume still works there. That puts it at medium, but the fix is tiny.
better_fix:
Three small changes; skip generated_at and the staleness rejection.
1. Plugin: hardening responses, and ideally every LSM route, send `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, either through the rest_send_nocache_headers filter for the lsm/v1 namespace or as a header on the response.
2. API: add a `_={microtime}` query parameter in LsmService::get() for all GETs. It is one line and also fixes backup/list.
3. Watchdog: never decide from a GET. For each overdue open row, POST /hardening/resume and close the row from that response. The call must be an idempotent no-op when nothing is paused.

title: hardening:resume-expired inherits the known stuck-mutex failure, runs serially at up to 150 s per row, has no escalation, and breaks on deleted/archived projects
scenario: (a) Spec says 'every 10 minutes (withoutOverlapping)'. Default expiry is 1440 min and every existing entry uses the default; the scheduler mutex stuck twice in the last month (25-28 Aug, 6-7 Sep, permanent fix still open). A Hostinger-killed CLI run leaves the mutex -> no platform resume for >=24 h, exactly the backstop for cached sites. (b) Per open row: status GET (30 s) + resume POST (120 s). Three unreachable sites = 7.5 min per run, forever ('leave open, retry next run' has no cap). Without runInBackground() this blocks schedule:run and delays sites:check-uptime spawned after it. (c) Project uses SoftDeletes: a project deleted while paused -> $pause->project is null -> LsmService::for(null) TypeError aborts the loop, so every later row is never processed. If the author copies the sibling convention `where('status','!=','archived')`, a project archived during a pause is never resumed. URL edited or health_check_secret rotated mid-pause -> calls go to the wrong site / get 401, handled as 'unreachable' forever. (d) The only signal is `pause_overdue` inside that one project's Security panel, which nobody has open.
evidence: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-api/routes/console.php:22-26,76-81 (conventions: withoutOverlapping() default + runInBackground + name + onOneServer), :144-147 (queue is sync); vendor/laravel/framework/src/Illuminate/Console/Scheduling/ManagesAttributes.php:145 ($expiresAt = 1440); app/Models/Project.php:18 (SoftDeletes); CheckSiteUptime.php:60-61 (archived filter convention); memory project_uptime_stale_statuses_aug28.md + project_pankobau_outage_sep2026.md (mutex stuck, fix open).
fix: Schedule as `->everyFiveMinutes()->withoutOverlapping(15)->runInBackground()->name('hardening-resume-expired')->onOneServer()`. In the command: eager-load `project` withTrashed and do NOT filter archived; snapshot url + secret into the pause row at pause time and call those; per-row try/catch; short timeouts (connect 5 s, resume 60 s) and Http::pool for parallelism; a hard per-run time budget. Escalate: when a row is >15 min overdue send a notification (infrastructure exists in app/Notifications) to admins + the pausing user, repeat hourly, and surface an 'overdue pauses' counter on the dashboard. Add a row state (open / resumed_by_plugin / resumed_by_platform / failed) instead of only resumed_at.
verifier:
(a) Real and cheap to fix. withoutOverlapping() defaults to 1440 min (ManagesAttributes.php:145). The stuck-mutex incident is documented in project_uptime_stale_statuses_aug28.md: confirmed cause, 3 days without uptime rows, and an open follow-up for a shorter expiry.
(b) Partly real. Serial status plus resume at 30+120 s per unreachable row has no cap. It needs unreachable sites that also have open pauses, which is rare.
(c) The SoftDeletes case is real. Project.php:18 uses SoftDeletes and LsmService::for(Project $project) is type-hinted, so a null relation throws a TypeError and aborts the loop. The 'author copies the archived filter' and 'URL or secret rotated mid-pause' parts are speculation. Copying url and health_check_secret into the pause row would duplicate a secret whose at-rest encryption is still pending, so I reject that part.
(d) True. pause_overdue is visible only inside one project's panel.
Overall this is medium, not high. The plugin self-resumes on the first PHP load, and the platform's own uptime probe guarantees one every interval even on fully cached sites. The watchdog is a backstop.
better_fix:
Schedule it as `->everyTenMinutes()->withoutOverlapping(15)->runInBackground()->name('hardening-resume-expired')->onOneServer()`. This matches routes/console.php:76-81 and adds a short mutex expiry.
In the command:
- Wrap each row in try/catch.
- Close a row whose project is trashed or missing, and note it.
- Use short timeouts: connect 5 s, resume 60 s.
- Stop retrying after 24 h. Mark the row failed and stop.
- Send one notification to the pausing user and the admins when a row is more than 30 min overdue. The existing Notification infrastructure plus a nullable overdue_notified_at column covers this.
Leave out Http::pool, hourly repeats, a dashboard counter, the url and secret snapshot, and a four-value row state enum.

title: Timeout chain (SPA 30 s default, API 120 s, plugin unbounded) plus row-after-call ordering can create a live pause that the platform has no record of; operations are not re-queryable
scenario: SPA axios default is 30 s; the existing long calls override to exactly 120000 ms, equal to the API->plugin timeout, so the browser gives up before the API can answer. User clicks 'Pause 60'. Plugin apply takes 40 s on a slow host. SPA shows 'timeout of 30000ms exceeded' (generic error toast, not 'Rolled back'). Meanwhile the plugin finished: backups are public. If the API writes the project_hardening_pauses row only after a successful plugin response (spec: 'A row is written on pause') and the platform request dies first (LiteSpeed gateway timeout under load, deploy/config:cache mid-request, LsmService::post() catching a cURL timeout and returning null -> controller 500), there is no row -> resume-expired never looks at this site. User retries: second pause either extends pause_until or hits the 120 s lock and is reported as 'unsupported'. last_result has no operation id, so the SPA cannot tell whether last_result belongs to its click, to a colleague's, or to a plugin-load re-apply. Also lock TTL, pending threshold and API timeout are all 120 s: an apply still running at 121 s gets crash-recovered by the next plugin load while it is still writing.
evidence: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-web/packages/api-client/src/client.ts:47 and src/lib/api.ts:46 (30000); src/lib/lsm-api.ts:167,173 (120000); LsmService.php:14 (UPDATE_TIMEOUT=120), :655-672 (exceptions -> null); LsmController has no set_time_limit on 120 s routes (only SecurityScanController.php:50 does). Spec: lock 120 s, crash recovery 'older than 120 s', 'POSTs use UPDATE_TIMEOUT (120 s)'.
fix: Write-ahead: insert the pause row (state=pending, paused_until, op_id) BEFORE calling the plugin; on explicit success:false close it as failed; on timeout/unknown leave it open so the watchdog reconciles. Pass a client-generated op_id SPA->API->plugin, store it in last_result; on SPA timeout poll GET status until last_result.op_id matches (max ~150 s) and show 'still working'. Set SPA timeout > API timeout > plugin apply budget (e.g. 150 s / 90 s / 45 s); lock TTL and crash-recovery threshold >= 2x the budget; ignore_user_abort(true) + set_time_limit in both the controller and the plugin apply. Define pause-while-paused semantics explicitly (idempotent with same op_id; otherwise extend only up to a cap).
verifier:
Verified: the SPA default timeout is 30000 ms (packages/api-client/src/client.ts:47, src/lib/api.ts:46), the long calls use 120000 ms (lsm-api.ts:167,173), and UPDATE_TIMEOUT is 120 (LsmService.php:14). The spec never bounds the plugin's loopback timeouts, so 'plugin unbounded' is a fair reading.
The real parts:
- If useHardening uses the default client, a slow apply shows a generic 30 s timeout even though the pause succeeded.
- 'A row is written on pause' says nothing about ordering. Writing the row after the call leaves a live pause with no row whenever the API request dies after the plugin has applied.
- A second pause while the lock is held comes back as 'unsupported'.
The overstated parts:
- Laravel keeps running after the browser gives up, so in the 40 s scenario the row does get written.
- On Linux max_execution_time does not count curl wait time.
- The 121 s crash-recovery race needs an apply that outlives 9 loopbacks. It goes away once loopbacks are bounded.
- The op_id plumbing plus SPA polling is overkill for an action that normally finishes in under 5 s.
The reviewer missed one case. A pause while already paused creates a second open row. When the first row expires, the watchdog finds the site 'still paused' and resumes it, which cuts the extended pause short.
better_fix:
1. Write-ahead: insert the pause row before calling the plugin. On an explicit success:false, close it as failed. On a timeout or unknown result, leave it open for the watchdog, whose resume POST is idempotent.
2. On each new pause, close any earlier open rows for the project, so there is one open row per project holding the latest paused_until. Prefer the plugin's returned pause_until.
3. Order the timeouts: plugin loopbacks 5 s each (about 45 s worst case), API 120 s, SPA 130 s for the three hardening POSTs. Keep the lock and crash-recovery thresholds at 120 s, which is now more than twice the budget.
4. Spec one sentence for pause-while-paused: set pause_until to now plus the requested minutes, with no file change.
No op_id, no polling, and no ignore_user_abort, which LSWS does not support anyway.

title: Status is specified from the option (desired state), but the file is what protects: several ordinary events make them diverge with no detection
scenario: (1) Crash recovery restores the snapshot but the spec does not reset `rules`, so after a PHP fatal mid-enable desired=on, file=unprotected, status 'on'. (2) AI1WM restore/migration (AI1WM is on 136 sites and is the very workflow this feature serves): DB option lsm_hardening comes from the backup, wp-content/.htaccess may or may not; restore to an nginx or differently configured host leaves option 'on' + block present but ineffective; restoring an older backup gives option 'off' while the block is still in the file -> panel says Off, no Pause button, AI1WM download still 403. (3) Someone edits wp-content/.htaccess over SSH or a self-restoring kit rewrites it (frozen Hostinger sites already carry a kit stub in wp-content/.htaccess). (4) Plugin resumed itself but the platform row is still open -> panel shows pause_overdue although site is protected; conversely if the plugin is unreachable the API's status call returns 500 and pause_overdue (platform-only knowledge) is never shown. The self-test runs only at apply time, so none of this is ever noticed.
evidence: Spec 'State' (rules = desired state), 'Crash recovery' (no mention of rules), 'GET /hardening/status -> per rule on|off|paused|manual|unsupported'. Kit stub in wp-content/.htaccess: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/wp-audits/midnightblue-duck-937654.hostingersite.com_2026-09-07/scan.txt ('--- wp-content/.htaccess ---' section: `<IfModule litespeed>` / `php_value` / `</IfModule>`). LsmController pattern returns 500 on null (e.g. LsmController.php:909-915).
fix: Status = f(file, option): parse the marker block on every status call and report per rule {desired, block_present, effective, verified_at}; add explicit states `drift` and `ineffective`. Re-verify (probe) on status when verified_at is older than N hours, rate-limited. Include a compact hardening summary in /health so the 3x/day deep health check can raise drift/ineffective/overdue without anyone opening the panel. API status endpoint must still answer from the pauses table when the plugin is unreachable ({reachable:false, open_pause, pause_overdue}). Close rows opportunistically whenever any fresh status shows not-paused + block present; compute overdue from plugin truth when reachable.
verifier:
Sub-issue (1) is a genuine spec bug in the same class as finding 1. Step 6 'set rules back to the previous desired state' implies `rules` is committed before the write. 'Crash recovery' restores only the file and clears `pending`. After a process death mid-enable the option says on, the file is unprotected, and status reads 'on'. Process death mid-apply is ordinary on LiteSpeed, because LSWS kills PHP when the client disconnects, so this is more than a rare fatal.
(2) and (3) are plausible. AI1WM is active on 136 sites and migrations move the option and the file independently. The team also hand-edits wp-content/.htaccess on the frozen Hostinger sites. The kit stub is confirmed in the midnightblue-duck scan_verify.txt.
(4) is real but mild. A false pause_overdue lasts at most one watchdog interval. The 500-on-null controller pattern (LsmController.php:909-915) does hide the platform's own pause knowledge when the plugin is unreachable.
The proposed fix is too big: drift and ineffective states, periodic re-probing on status, and a /health summary.
better_fix:
1. Commit `rules` and `pause_until` to the option only in step 7, after the self-test passes, and build the block from the candidate state held in memory. Crash recovery then has nothing to revert. If that is awkward, store prev_rules and prev_pause_until in `pending` and restore them.
2. Status reads the file. Run extract_from_markers() on each status call, which is one small file read. A rule is 'on' only if it is desired and its lines are in the managed block. Otherwise report one extra value, `drift`, which offers re-enable.
3. The API status endpoint still answers from the pauses table when the plugin is unreachable ({reachable:false, open_pause, pause_overdue}). It closes an open row opportunistically when a fresh plugin response shows not paused.
Defer the effective re-probe, the verified_at ageing and the /health integration. A manual 'Verify now' button can come later if drift shows up in practice.

title: LsmService collapses 404/401/timeout/5xx into null, so 'plugin older than 2.10.0' shows as a generic 500 on the whole fleet during rollout, and success:false handling is asymmetric
scenario: API and web deploy the same day; plugins update only when WP auto-update or someone's 'update all' runs (inventory still shows 2.9.3, 2.9.2 and even 2.6.0 in the fleet; the platform does not persist plugin version). Every Security panel calls GET /hardening -> plugin answers 404 rest_no_route -> handleResponse() returns null -> controller convention returns 500 'Failed to ...' -> the new card shows a red error on ~141 sites; the spec's status enum has no value for this. The same collapse makes the watchdog treat a rotated API key (401) or a 404 as 'unreachable, retry forever'. For POSTs: on success handleResponse() unwraps to `data` (no `success` key), on success:false it returns the raw envelope, so 'check success explicitly' must special-case shape; any dev following the existing `if (!$result) 500` pattern will return rolled-back changes as HTTP 200. The SPA only reads `response.data.message`, while LsmController errors use the `error` key, so the 422 reason would render as 'Request failed with status code 422'.

title: 'Exact match' adoption will miss the manual rules actually deployed — including on the motivating site — making pause impossible exactly where it is needed
scenario: The audit procedure text today appends `<FilesMatch "\.php$">` + `Deny from all`, but drjung.ch (one of the two sites named in the spec's Problem section) actually carries `<FilesMatch "\.php$">` + `Require all denied`. The procedure was edited several times (incidents.md documents the earlier bare `>>` version), so archive-rule variants (different extension list, with/without IfModule) certainly exist on sites cleaned earlier. On such a site: status shows 'off' although the rule is effective; enabling duplicates the rule and reports 'on'; the first 'Pause for download' is rolled back with pause_ineffective_foreign_rule and the team is back to SSH/SFTP — the exact problem the feature was built to remove. An admin 'disable' reports Off while the foreign rule still blocks.
evidence: ~/.claude/skills/wordpress-security-audit/SKILL.md:343-350 and :376-380 (current blocks) vs ~/.claude/skills/wordpress-security-audit/audits/drjung.ch_2026-09-10/scan_verify.txt:287-290 (deployed variant). Spec 'Manual rules already on a site': 'whitespace-normalised exact match ... Anything not matching exactly is never touched'.
fix: Before release, inventory real wp-content/.htaccess and uploads/.htaccess contents fleet-wide (the scan collector already ships them: class-lsm-scan-collector.php:152-180) and build the recogniser from that corpus. Recognise a small grammar instead of exact text: a standalone <Files|FilesMatch> block whose only directives are Require all denied / Deny from all / Order, with optional IfModule wrappers, whose pattern is a subset of our extension list. Add status `foreign` (probe blocked before we wrote anything, no recognised block) with the offending file/lines returned so the panel can say what to remove. Ship the audit-procedure change (write inside LSM-HARDENING markers or call the toggle) together with 2.10.0, not as a later follow-up, otherwise every new cleanup creates another variant.
verifier:
This has the strongest evidence in the set. Both audited sites I could inspect carry blocks that do not match the current procedure text.
- midnightblue-duck's wp-content/.htaccess (scan_verify.txt ~l.318-327) has `<Files "debug.log">` and `<FilesMatch "\.(wpress|sql|zip|tar|gz|bak)$">`, each with a bare `Require all denied` and no IfModule wrapper. SKILL.md:376-380 now writes an IfModule-wrapped version of the archive block, and the debug.log block in SKILL.md (~l.343-350) uses `Deny from all`.
- drjung.ch's uploads/.htaccess has `Require all denied`, where SKILL.md (~l.343-350) has `Deny from all`.
The spec's 'whitespace-normalised exact match' against 'the exact blocks the audit procedure appends' would miss these blocks on these sites. The consequence chain follows from the spec text. Status shows 'off' while the rule is effective, enabling duplicates the rule, and the first pause is rolled back with pause_ineffective_foreign_rule. That sends the team back to SSH on the legacy cleaned sites, which are the only sites with the problem today.
There is no safety harm, but it defeats the primary goal on day one. I rate it high on feature value.
better_fix:
Recognise a small grammar, about 20 lines of matcher, in place of exact text.
- The opening line must equal one of the three known patterns after whitespace normalisation: `<Files "debug.log">`, `<FilesMatch "\.php$">`, or `<FilesMatch "\.(wpress|sql|zip|tar|gz|bak)$">`.
- The body may contain only lines from {Require all denied, Deny from all, Order deny,allow, Order allow,deny, <IfModule mod_authz_core.c>, <IfModule !mod_authz_core.c>, </IfModule>}.
- Then the matching close tag.
Use the deployed blocks from the audit artifacts (midnightblue-duck, drjung.ch) as test fixtures. Before release, pull wp-content/.htaccess and uploads/.htaccess for the fleet once through the existing scan collector (class-lsm-scan-collector.php:152-180) and check that every manual block is recognised. That is a test step and needs no new code.
Skip a separate `foreign` status. pause_ineffective_foreign_rule already covers the residue, if it returns the offending file path.
Ship the audit-procedure change (write inside the LSM-HARDENING markers or use the toggle) with 2.10.0. It is a text edit to SKILL.md.

title: 'Applied and verified' is proven with a .bak file in wp-content root — not representative for nginx-fronted hosts nor for where AI1WM backups actually live
scenario: (a) nginx-fronted Apache (Plesk-style 'serve static files directly'): the static extension list contains zip/gz/tar/tgz but not bak/wpress/sql. The .bak probe is proxied to Apache -> 403 -> 'verified', while wp-content/*.zip and *.gz are served by nginx and remain public. The drjung.ch report already notes 'nginx front-end may not honor .htaccess for static paths'. (b) AI1WM stores backups in get_option('ai1wm_backups_path'); if that is outside wp-content but inside ABSPATH, AI1WM links downloads via site_url and our wp-content/.htaccess never applies: panel shows On/verified, backups public. (c) Pause verification has the mirror problem: the .bak-in-root probe returning 200 does not prove the real ai1wm-backups/*.wpress URL is downloadable. Checked for conflicts: AI1WM's own ai1wm-backups/.htaccess contains only AddType/DirectoryIndex/Options -Indexes (no Require/Allow/Deny), so the parent deny IS inherited, a pause IS needed, and AI1WM rewriting that file on every admin_init does not override or touch ours.
evidence: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LocalWordpress/baucubmedia/wp-content/plugins/all-in-one-wp-migration/constants.php:395,503; functions.php:369-386 (ai1wm_backup_url, site_url branch); lib/model/class-ai1wm-backups.php:173-189; lib/vendor/servmask/filesystem/class-ai1wm-file-htaccess.php:40-58; lib/controller/class-ai1wm-main-controller.php:82,260-262; lib/view/backups/backups-list.php:107-109 (direct href download). drjung report_dev line 42.
fix: Probe one tiny file per class that matters: .wpress, .zip and .sql (not only .bak); report per-extension results and a `partial` state instead of a single verified flag. When AI1WM is installed, place the .wpress probe inside the real AI1WM_BACKUPS_PATH (if under ABSPATH) for both enable and pause verification; if the path is outside wp-content return warning `archives_outside_scope` so the panel does not claim protection. Expose `server` plus a detected `static_frontend` hint (Server response header of the probe differs from SERVER_SOFTWARE).
verifier:
(a) is confirmed against the vendor docs. Plesk's 'Serve static files directly by nginx' default list contains gz, tar, tgz, zip and rar, but not bak, wpress or sql. For listed extensions the requests never reach Apache, so .htaccess directives are not applied (https://www.plesk.com/kb/docs/apache-and-nginx-settings-serve-only-files-with-specific-extensions-via-nginx/). On such a host a .bak probe goes through Apache and returns 403, the panel says 'verified', and *.zip and *.gz stay public. The drjung.ch report (line 42) already notes an nginx front-end. It is not the Plesk default, so likelihood is moderate. AI1WM .wpress files would still be blocked there. The exposure is zips: UpdraftPlus on 16 sites, Duplicator, and stray installer zips.
(c) is real in mirror image. A pausable .bak does not prove .wpress is downloadable if a foreign rule targets only wpress.
(b) is not substantiated for this fleet. AI1WM_BACKUPS_PATH defaults to wp-content/ai1wm-backups (constants.php). A relocated path needs a deliberate option change, and today's manual rule has the same gap. The AI1WM-internals finding (the ai1wm-backups/.htaccess has no authz directives, so the parent deny is inherited) checks out in class-ai1wm-file-htaccess.php:40-58.
better_fix:
Change the probe extensions. Do not add states.
- The enable check creates lsm-probe-<rand>.zip, the extension most likely to bypass Apache, and lsm-probe-<rand>.wpress. Both must return 403.
- The pause check requires the .wpress probe not to return 403.
That is one extra loopback. If .zip is served directly, the result is the existing rule_ineffective rollback, which is honest.
No `partial` state, no AI1WM path discovery, and no static_frontend hint. If anyone ever relocates ai1wm_backups_path, handle it then.

title: Security score ignores hardening (or would punish unsupported hosts), and the card's EN+DE i18n lands in a section that has no i18n at all
scenario: controlsScore is a fixed 7 x 100/7 sum over securitySettings. A site whose backups are publicly downloadable (rule off, paused, drifted or pause overdue) still scores 100 and renders green — the score contradicts the new card. If someone 'fixes' that by adding three more controls, Raidboxes/nginx sites (permanently `unsupported`) and sites in a legitimate 15-min pause drop in score through no fault of the team. Separately: SecuritySection.tsx contains no useTranslation/t() at all (all strings hard-coded English, toast built from the setting key), so a German user gets one translated card inside an English section; plugin reason codes (asset_broken, rule_ineffective, pause_ineffective_foreign_rule, loopback_blocked, future codes from newer plugins) need a mapping with fallback; the pause countdown computed from unix pause_until against the browser clock is wrong when the client or site clock is off.
evidence: /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-web/src/features/projects/components/sections/SecuritySection.tsx:227-240 (controlsScore), :129-141 (hard-coded messages), no useTranslation import in the file; i18n lives in the monolith src/lib/i18n.ts.
fix: Add hardening to `securityChecks` (not controls) as outcome-based checks using `effective`: pass when effective (managed, manual or foreign), warning when off/paused, fail when overdue/drift, and excluded from the denominator when unsupported. Spec the i18n scope explicitly (new card only, keys under projects.security.hardening.*, reason-code map with raw-code fallback and EN default). Have the API return `seconds_remaining` computed from the plugin's own clock and count down from that.
verifier:
The facts are verified. controlsScore is a fixed 7 x 100/7 sum (SecuritySection.tsx:227-240). The file has no useTranslation and hard-codes English, with the toast built from the setting key (:129-141). The client-clock countdown skew is real but trivial.
None of this is an integration defect. The spec never claims the score reflects hardening, and the reviewer notes that adding it to the score would punish hosts that are permanently `unsupported`. The mixed-language section is cosmetic.
better_fix:
Add one line to the spec: 'the security score is unchanged in v1'. Then:
- i18n for the new card only, with keys under projects.security.hardening.*.
- A reason-code label map that falls back to the raw code, so newer plugins do not break the UI.
- The API returns seconds_remaining, computed from the plugin's pause_until and the plugin-reported time, and the card counts down from that. No outcome-based score checks.

title: Containment-freeze sites: no rule conflict, but the persistent whole-file snapshot collides with the audit scanner and with concurrent SSH edits
scenario: Confirmed no conflict with the Hostinger freeze: the auto_prepend line is in the ROOT .htaccess inside <IfModule litespeed>, its target wp-content/e8cbcc15.php is included via the filesystem (HTTP authz in wp-content/.htaccess is irrelevant), none of our patterns match .php in wp-content, and insert_with_markers preserves the kit stub already present in wp-content/.htaccess. Two side effects though: (1) the snapshot `wp-content/.htaccess.lsm-bak` is never deleted in step 7; the audit scanner's A1.11 rule flags any dotfile in wp-content other than .htaccess/.litespeed_conf.dat as HIGH, so every hardened site fails the next audit's scan_diff gate with a false IOC. (2) Rollback/crash-recovery restore the WHOLE file: on the ~75 frozen sites the team is actively editing wp-content/.htaccess over SSH (removing kit stubs); an apply that crashed before such an edit and is 'recovered' on the next plugin load silently resurrects the old content, and a lingering lsm-probe-*.php in uploads after a PHP fatal (finally does not run on timeouts) is flagged by the LSM weekly scan ('PHP file in uploads directory') and by Wordfence (133 sites).
evidence: scan.txt of midnightblue-duck (root .htaccess `php_value auto_prepend_file ".../wp-content/e8cbcc15.php"` inside <IfModule litespeed>; wp-content/.htaccess stub); ~/.claude/skills/wordpress-security-audit/SKILL.md:135 (A1.11), :141 (A2.4); /Users/bmarkovic/Documents/Projects/LSMPlatform/lsm-wp/landeseiten-maintenance/includes/class-lsm-security-scanner.php:133-156 (PHP in uploads finding). Spec steps 3, 6, 7 and 'Crash recovery'.
fix: Delete the snapshot in step 7 (keep it only while `pending` is set) and record its sha1 + the pre-write sha1 of the live file in `pending`; crash recovery restores only if the live file still equals what we wrote (otherwise do a marker-scoped removal via insert_with_markers with the previous block and report `crash_recovered_file_changed`). Crash recovery also deletes any lsm-probe-* leftovers. Whitelist `.htaccess.lsm-bak` and `lsm-probe-*` in the audit scanner's A1.11/uploads-PHP checks, and add a line to the audit procedure's hardening step that these names are ours.
verifier:
Verified:
- Step 7 of the spec never deletes `.htaccess.lsm-bak`. Audit rule A1.11 (SKILL.md:135) flags any wp-content dotfile other than .htaccess and .litespeed_conf.dat as HIGH. Every hardened site would produce a false IOC at its next audit.

- I also checked the platform scanner's htaccess signatures (config/scanner_signatures.php:95-104). They do not match our block.
- The no-conflict analysis for the Hostinger freeze is correct.
The whole-file-restore versus concurrent-SSH-edit scenario needs a crash and a hand edit of the same file within the recovery window. That is too unlikely to justify sha1 bookkeeping and a second recovery mode.

1. Delete the snapshot in step 7, on success and after a rollback. It exists only while `pending` is set.
2. Crash recovery also unlinks any lsm-probe-* files in both directories.
3. Add the two filenames to the audit skill's A1.11 allow-list and to the hardening step. That is a text edit.
Accept the concurrent-SSH-edit risk and add one line to the freeze runbook: do not toggle hardening while hand-editing wp-content/.htaccess.
